record.paper_title: Open Problems in Data-Sharing Peer-to-Peer Systems
record.original_question: Given existing peer-to-peer techniques for COUNT queries over predicates, can those methods be extended to support more expressive aggregate queries, including SUM, MAX, and MEDIAN, over decentralized data-sharing systems?

evidence.quote: Further research is needed to extend these techniques into more expressive aggregates like SUM, MAX, and MEDIAN.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a decentralized data-sharing system modeled as a peer-to-peer network in which each peer p in a set P stores a local relation R_p over a common schema. For a predicate φ defining a subset S_φ = { t ∈ ⋃_{p∈P} R_p : φ(t) holds } of tuples distributed across the network, suppose there exist distributed protocols that, without centralizing the data and tolerating churn and partial failures, compute the aggregate COUNT(S_φ) = |S_φ| approximately or exactly with bounded message, bandwidth, and round complexity.

The problem is to determine whether such peer-to-peer protocols for COUNT can be generalized to compute the following aggregates over S_φ on a designated numeric attribute a:
  (i) SUM(S_φ) = Σ_{t ∈ S_φ} t.a,
  (ii) MAX(S_φ) = max_{t ∈ S_φ} t.a,
  (iii) MEDIAN(S_φ) = the order statistic of rank ⌈|S_φ|/2⌉ of the multiset { t.a : t ∈ S_φ }.

Specifically, design distributed algorithms that evaluate SUM, MAX, and MEDIAN over a fully decentralized peer-to-peer network, establish their correctness (exact or with provable approximation guarantees), and analyze their communication, computation, and round complexity in the presence of dynamic membership, replication, and possible faulty or adversarial peers.
artifact.status_search_result: A targeted search was not performed in detail, but the broader research area of distributed/gossip-based aggregation in peer-to-peer systems has seen substantial work (e.g., gossip aggregation, sketches for SUM, approximate quantiles for MEDIAN, and distributed top-k for MAX). However, whether the specific question of fully extending the referenced COUNT-style techniques to SUM, MAX, and MEDIAN with comparable guarantees has been definitively resolved is unclear, so the status is reported as unknown.
